title: Listening: Paraphrasing a Poem You Hear
summary: The three-phase technique for understanding a poem from listening alone: first listen, second listen for key devices, then paraphrase from figurative to literal language.

p: Paraphrasing a poem that you only hear is harder than paraphrasing written drama, because the sound disappears as soon as it is spoken. You must catch the essence of the poem from its sound and performance.
Goal: understand the overall mood and subject. Do not get stuck on difficult words. Ask: What is the dominant feeling (tone)? What is the poem mainly about (love, loss, nature, injustice)?

Goal: notice the poet's tools. Listen for key images (the pictures the poet creates, such as a lone tree in a barren field or a noisy market), figurative language (metaphor, simile and personification) and repetition of words or phrases for emphasis. Jot down key images and phrases as you hear them.

Metaphor: one thing is said to be another (Hope is the thing with feathers). Simile: a comparison using like or as (My love is like a red, red rose). Personification: giving human qualities to a non-human thing (The wind whispered).
Turn the poet's artistic language into clear, plain prose that explains the meaning.
Heard: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul. Paraphrase: Hope is a strong and lasting feeling that lives inside a person.
Heard: My love is like a red, red rose. Paraphrase: The speaker thinks his love is extremely beautiful and delicate.

activity: Ask a friend to read a short poem twice. Write the tone and subject after the first reading; list three images after the second; then write a paraphrase of two or three sentences.

title: Reading: Summarising by Outlining Main Points
summary: A step-by-step method: find the thesis, find each topic sentence, build a skeleton outline with Roman numerals and capital letters, and then write a flowing summary.

p: Outlining is a very effective way to make a precise and logical summary, because it makes you see the structure of the passage.
Step 1: find the thesis, the central argument or main message, usually in the introduction or conclusion. Ask: What is the one thing the author most wants me to understand?
Step 2: read each body paragraph and find its topic sentence (the main idea), often the first or last sentence.

Step 3: make a skeleton outline. Put the thesis at the top as a title. Use Roman numerals (I, II, III) for the main points (the topic sentences) and capital letters (A, B, C) for the key supporting details.
Step 4: write the summary. Turn the outline into flowing prose in your own words, joining the points with transitions.
Thesis: Corruption is a major obstacle to national development.
I. Diversion of public funds. A. Money for schools and hospitals is stolen. B. This increases poverty and inequality.
II. Loss of public trust in government. A. It leads to widespread cynicism. B. It encourages lawlessness.
III. Foreign investors stay away. A. The nation seems unstable and unpredictable.

Summary: Corruption severely hinders national development. Firstly, it leads to the diversion of public funds, depriving citizens of essential services and worsening poverty. Secondly, it erodes public trust in government, fostering cynicism and lawlessness. Finally, it deters foreign investment, because the nation is seen as unstable.

activity: Find a 300-word newspaper article on a social issue (for example the effect of social media on young people). Write a formal outline with a thesis, three main points (I, II, III) and supporting points (A, B), then write a 60-word summary from it.

title: Vocabulary: Latin and Greek Roots
summary: Common Latin and Greek roots that help you decode unfamiliar words, with examples and practice.

p: A large part of advanced English comes from Latin and Greek roots, prefixes and suffixes. If you know the roots you can guess the meaning of unfamiliar words in the examination and improve your vocabulary quickly.

aqua- (water): aquarium, aquatic, aquifer. port- (carry): transport, portable, export, portfolio. scrib- or script- (write): scribe, describe, manuscript, prescription. terra- (earth): territory, terrain, terrestrial, subterranean. mal- (bad): malpractice, malignant, malice, malnourished. bene- (good): benefactor, benefit, benevolent, benign.

bio- (life): biology, biography, antibiotic, biosphere. tele- (far): telescope, telephone, television, telepathy. graph- or gram- (write, draw): autograph, biography, diagram, grammar. -logy (study of): biology, geology, psychology, anthropology. phon- (sound): telephone, symphony, microphone, phonics. chron- (time): chronological, chronic, synchronise, chronicle.

Chronograph: chron- (time) + -graph (write or record) = a device that records time precisely, such as a stopwatch. Aquaphobia: aqua- (water) + -phobia (fear) = an irrational fear of water. Malnutrition: mal- (bad) + nutrition = poor nourishment. Benefactor: bene- (good) + factor (one who does) = a person who does good, especially by giving money. Telegraph: tele- (far) + -graph (write) = writing over a long distance.
Break the word into parts. Find a part you know. Check the sentence for support. Example: The aquifer under the desert supplies water to the town. Aqua- tells you the aquifer has to do with water.

activity: Give the meaning of: biography (writing about a life), telescope (instrument to see far), malpractice (bad practice), subterranean (under the earth), benevolent (wishing good), geology (study of the earth).

title: Writing: Revising an Expository Essay
summary: A six-point checklist for improving a first draft: thesis, unity, evidence, coherence, tone and conclusion.

p: Revision is looking at your draft again with a critical eye. It turns a good essay into an excellent one by improving clarity, logic and impact. Leave your draft for a while, then read it as if someone else wrote it.
a. Thesis: is it specific, clearly stated in the introduction and a reliable map of the whole essay?
b. Paragraph unity: does each body paragraph begin with a strong topic sentence that supports the thesis? Is every sentence in the paragraph about that topic?

c. Evidence: have you moved beyond vague statements to concrete examples, facts and reasons? Instead of Drug abuse is bad, write Drug abuse leads to specific health problems such as liver cirrhosis and mental illness.
d. Coherence and transitions: do ideas flow from one to the next? Use transitions such as furthermore, consequently, in contrast and as a result.
e. Formal, objective tone: remove personal opinions (I think, I believe) and informal language (slang, contractions). Keep the tone academic.
f. Conclusion: does it restate the thesis in different words and summarise the main points without adding new information? Does it end with a strong final thought?
Spelling, punctuation, capital letters, verb tenses and subject-verb agreement. Read the essay aloud: your ear will catch mistakes that your eye misses. Check the word limit.

title: Grammar: Adjectival Clauses (Defining and Non-Defining)
summary: Relative clauses that describe nouns, the difference between defining and non-defining clauses, and how to punctuate them.

p: An adjectival (relative) clause is a dependent clause that tells us more about a noun or pronoun. It is introduced by who, whom, whose, which or that.

A defining clause gives information that is essential for identifying the noun: it tells us which one we mean. If you remove it, the meaning changes. No commas are used. Example: The student who top-scored in the exam received a scholarship. (Without the clause we do not know which student.) Tip: if you can put that in place of who or which, it is probably defining.

A non-defining clause gives extra, non-essential information about a noun that is already identified. It can be removed without changing the basic meaning. It must be separated by commas. Example: Mr. Bello, who is our Mathematics teacher, is travelling to a conference. (We already know who Mr. Bello is.) That cannot be used for a non-defining clause.

a. The man who lives next door is a doctor. (defining; no commas.) b. Mr. Adebayo, who is our maths teacher, is travelling today. (non-defining; commas.) c. The car that I bought last week has broken down. (defining; no commas.) d. Lagos, which is the economic hub of Nigeria, has a population of over 20 million. (non-defining; commas.)

activity: Add commas where needed: My sister who lives in Abuja is a pilot (if you have only one sister: My sister, who lives in Abuja, is a pilot). The book that you lent me was excellent (no commas). Explain how the first sentence changes if you have several sisters (no commas: it identifies which sister).

title: Vocabulary: Law and Order (Part 1)
summary: Words about the police, courts and legal process: police, plaintiff, defendant, tribunal, justice, civil rights and societal norms.

p: After the midterm, we study the language of justice and social order. It is important for discussing crime, justice and civic responsibility accurately.
Police: the civil force of a state responsible for preventing and detecting crime and keeping public order.

Plaintiff: the party who begins a lawsuit in a civil court; the person who says he has been wronged and asks for a legal remedy such as compensation. Example: The plaintiff sued the company for damages after he slipped on a wet floor.
Defendant: the person, company or institution against whom a civil or criminal case is brought. Example: The defendant stood silently in the dock while the charges were read.

Tribunal: a body set up to settle certain kinds of dispute, often less formal than a full court but with legal authority, such as an Industrial Tribunal or an Election Petitions Tribunal. Example: The dispute between landlord and tenant was settled by a rent tribunal.

Justice: (1) the quality of being fair and reasonable, and the use of law to keep it (The families of the victims cried out for justice); (2) a judge of a superior court (The ruling was delivered by Justice Amina Augie).

Civil rights: the rights of citizens to political and social freedom and equality, protecting them from unfair treatment by the state or by other individuals. Example: The right to vote is a fundamental civil right.

Societal norms: the unwritten, shared rules about behaviour in a society. They are different from laws but powerfully guide conduct. Example: Queuing in an orderly way is a societal norm in many cultures.

activity: In a civil lawsuit, who is the plaintiff and who is the defendant? (The plaintiff brings the case; the defendant is sued.) What is the difference between a tribunal and a conventional court? (A tribunal is a special body for certain disputes, usually less formal than a full court.)

title: Vocabulary: Law and Order (Part 2)
summary: Litigation, verdict, acquitted, convicted, barrister and solicitor, and listening practice with a new poem.

p: Litigation: the process of taking legal action, suing someone or defending a lawsuit. Example: The company faced years of litigation over the damage it caused to the environment.
Verdict: the formal decision of a jury or judge on the facts at the end of a trial. Example: After three days, the jury returned a guilty verdict.
Acquitted: formally declared not guilty of a criminal charge. Example: Because of lack of evidence, the accused was acquitted and set free.
Convicted: formally found guilty of a criminal offence. Example: He was convicted of fraud and sentenced to five years in prison.

Barrister and solicitor: in the British legal system, which has influenced Nigeria's, a solicitor usually gives legal advice and prepares documents, while a barrister is a specialist advocate who speaks for clients in the higher courts.

Acquitted means found not guilty; convicted means found guilty. A verdict is the decision of guilt or innocence; a sentence is the punishment. A judge is the person who presides in court; a jury is a group of citizens who give the verdict (in Nigeria, most trials are decided by a judge alone).

Use the three-phase technique from the last lesson on a new poem that your teacher reads: first listen for tone and subject; second listen for key images and figurative language; then paraphrase into plain prose.

title: Writing: A Letter to the Editor
summary: The complete format of a formal letter to a newspaper editor, with a model letter on a community problem.

p: A letter to the editor is a formal letter by a citizen giving an informed opinion on a matter of public interest. It is a powerful way to take part in civic life.
1. Your address and the date: top right-hand corner. Example: 15, Educational Lane, Sabo, Yaba, Lagos State. 20th May, 2025.
2. The editor's address: left-hand side, below your address. Example: The Editor, The Guardian Newspapers, Isolo, Lagos State.
3. Salutation: formal and general: Dear Sir, or Dear Madam, (if you do not know the editor's sex, Dear Sir or Madam is also correct).
4. Title or heading: a short, strong phrase in capital letters or bold that sums up your argument. Example: THE MENACE OF EROSION ON AJAO ROAD.

5. The body: Paragraph 1 states your purpose and main point at once. Paragraphs 2 and 3 give specific details, evidence and consequences, using facts and logic. Paragraph 4 gives a clear recommendation or call to action: what should be done, and by whom?
6. Sign-off: Yours faithfully, (with a comma), your signature and your full printed name. Your town is optional.

Paragraph 1: I am writing through your esteemed newspaper to bring to the urgent attention of the Lagos State Government and the relevant authorities the deplorable state of Ajao Road, which has been made worse by severe erosion.

Paragraphs 2 and 3: The deep gullies have become a danger to motorists and pedestrians. Just last week a commercial motorcyclist was injured. Furthermore, the erosion is moving close to the foundations of houses.
Paragraph 4: I therefore urge the State Ministry of Works to send a team at once to assess the situation and begin repairs before a major tragedy occurs.

activity: Write a letter to the editor of about 150 words on a problem in your community (for example poor waste disposal or youth unemployment). Follow the six parts of the format exactly.

title: Grammar: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
summary: The three sentence types, the three kinds of subordinate clause (adverbial, adjectival and noun) and how to identify them.

p: A simple sentence has one independent clause (a subject and a verb that make a complete thought): The lawyer presented her case.

A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so: FANBOYS) or a semicolon: The lawyer presented her case, and the judge listened attentively.

A complex sentence has one independent (main) clause and at least one subordinate (dependent) clause. The subordinate clause cannot stand alone; it depends on the main clause: Although the evidence was strong, the defendant was acquitted. (Subordinate: Although the evidence was strong. Main: the defendant was acquitted.)
Adverbial clause: does the work of an adverb. The case was adjourned because a key witness was ill.
Adjectival clause: does the work of an adjective. The barrister who led the prosecution was very skilled.
Noun clause: does the work of a noun, as subject, object or complement. What the witness said shocked the courtroom. (subject)
The jury deliberated until they reached a verdict. The subordinate clause until they reached a verdict is adverbial (of time).
a. He left the courtroom after the verdict was announced. Subordinate clause: after the verdict was announced (adverbial, time).
b. The evidence that the prosecutor presented was irrefutable. Subordinate clause: that the prosecutor presented (adjectival).
c. I do not know why the judge dismissed the case. Subordinate clause: why the judge dismissed the case (noun clause, the object of know).

activity: Write one simple, one compound and one complex sentence about a school event. For the complex one, underline the subordinate clause and name its type.
